canonical_question: How does the 'negative slope' in the strain rate vs. thickness plot correlate with the specific strain rate values (e.g., 400 vs 1800 s^-1)?

question_variants.question: How does the 'negative slope' in the strain rate vs. thickness plot correlate with the specific strain rate values (e.g., 400 vs 1800 s^-1)?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The negative slope in the strain rate vs. thickness (or oxidation resistance) plot correlates with higher strain rates yielding higher oxidation resistance (implied by lower thickness or mass gain, though the text explicitly links the negative slope to 'higher oxidation resistance').

answers.answer: The negative slope indicates that samples processed at higher strain rates exhibit higher oxidation resistance.
answers.measurement_outcome: Higher oxidation resistance at higher strain rates
answers.boundary_limitation: Specific numerical strain rate values (400 vs 1800) are implied to follow this trend
evidence_spans: A coarse grain microstructure having BCC/B2 phases was obtained in the as-cast HEA sample.
Only 5 min of straining of sample significantly refined the grain structure from 98 to 1 μm and 0.43 μm for the SFP_400 and SFP_1800 sample, respectively.
The ultrafine-grained samples showed a phase transition from BCC/B2 to FCC structure.

source_evidence_spans: The trend of the curve shows a negative slope, which indicates higher oxidation resistance of the samples processed at higher strain rates
